docs.title: Count people, not motion.
docs.text:
Apex Crosswalk counts people as they enter and leave, so your lights, heating, and fans respond to real occupancy. Private, local, and energy efficient.

  • Step 1 Crosswalk Gateway Start here

  • Step 2 Crosswalk Sensor Once your Gateway is online

  • Apex CoreComing Soon

Scanned the QR code? You'll also need a computer

You can follow this guide on your phone, but to install the firmware you'll need Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac. When you get to a flashing step, open docs.apexsensorlabs.com on your computer and continue there.

Privacy Focused. Energy Savings. No Subscriptions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and Help
docs.text: If you're having issues with your Apex hardware, we're here to help. Because our devices are designed for local-first, privacy-focused home automation, most issues can be resolved with a few simple steps.

docs.title: Common Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Before reaching out, please check the following:

  • Connectivity: Ensure your Gateway is powered on, connected to your home Wi-Fi, and within range of your sensors.
  • Power: For battery-powered sensors, plug the sensor into USB and check that it charges — 🟡 Yellow means charging, 🟢 Green means full. For hardwired sensors, check that the 🔴 Red and 🟢 Green lights are on; if they're off, check the USB-C cable and power adapter.
  • Firmware: Ensure your device is running the latest firmware. The Gateway can update itself from its dashboard.

docs.title: Quick Fixes
docs.text:
• Gateway Issues: For Wi-Fi, dashboard, or MQTT problems, see the Crosswalk Gateway Troubleshooting Guide.
  • Sensor Issues: For count inaccuracies, pairing failures, or orientation help, refer to the Crosswalk Sensor Troubleshooting Guide.
  • Checking Sensor Status: Crosswalk sensor lights only show power, not pairing or counting, so the sensor light reference explains what you can and cannot tell from the hardware itself.

Common Suggestions

  • Reboot: Sometimes a simple power cycle (unplug and replug) is all that's needed to bring the Gateway back onto the network.
  • Proximity: When pairing new sensors, keep them in the same room as the Gateway for the most reliable initial handshake.
  • Dashboard First: The apex.local dashboard is the fastest way to see what every sensor and room is currently reporting.

A Note on Privacy

Apex Sensor Labs hardware does not have a cloud portal. This means we cannot "remotely access" your device to troubleshoot it. All support happens through local debugging on your own network, with us walking you through it.

docs.title: Reporting Issues
docs.text:
During the Crosswalk beta, email is the fastest way to reach us. Please include:

  • Which device you're having trouble with (Gateway or Sensor)
  • The firmware version shown on your apex.local dashboard

  • What you expected to happen, and what happened instead

  • Email: support@apexsensorlabs.com

  • Website: apexsensorlabs.com

DIY Community

A community space for Apex users to share automations and setups is on the way. Until then, email us — beta feedback goes straight to the engineer building the hardware.

docs.title: Getting Started with Apex Crosswalk
docs.text:
Set up your Gateway first

Your sensors talk to the Crosswalk Gateway, not directly to your Wi-Fi. A sensor can't pair or report counts until the Gateway is set up and online. If you haven't done that yet, start with the Gateway and come back here afterwards.

docs.title: Count people, not motion.
docs.text:
Apex Crosswalk counts people as they enter and leave, so your lights, heating, and fans respond to real occupancy. Private, local, and energy efficient.

By counting people as they pass through a doorway, it eliminates the "ghosting" and delays associated with traditional motion sensors.

docs.title: Unboxing
docs.text:
The Crosswalk Sensor is a high-precision occupancy detector. It comes in two versions:

  • Battery-Powered: Runs for months on a rechargeable battery, with no wires to the doorway.
  • Hardwired: Stays plugged into USB-C power, so there is no battery to charge.

Your sensor arrives fully assembled in its case. There is nothing to put together.

Battery-PoweredHardwired
  • 1x Crosswalk Sensor: Featuring dual sensing zones, assembled in its case.
  • 1x LiPo Battery: Already inside the case. You'll plug it in during pairing.
  • 2x Adhesive Mounting Strips: In the sensor bag. Keep these for mounting.
  • USB-C Charging Cable NOT included
  • 1x Crosswalk Sensor: Featuring dual sensing zones, assembled in its case.
  • 2x Adhesive Mounting Strips: In the sensor bag. Keep these for mounting.
  • USB-C Cable and USB Power Adapter NOT included

docs.title: Setup Process
docs.text:
Follow the linear walkthrough to get your Crosswalk sensor up and running.

You'll need a computer for Step 1

To flash the sensor, you'll need Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac.

  • Start Step 1: Flashing

docs.title: Step 1: Attach the Antenna
docs.text:
Your Crosswalk Gateway comes almost ready to go. The only thing you need to do before setup is attach the antenna, which the Gateway uses to talk to your Wi-Fi and your Crosswalk sensors.

No need to open the case

The small adapter inside the case is already installed. You only need to attach the external antenna.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• Crosswalk Gateway
  • 2.4GHz Antenna (in the box)

docs.title: Attaching the Antenna
docs.text:
1. Find the Connector: Look for the gold, threaded connector on the end of the Gateway case.

  2. Screw on the Antenna: Line the antenna up with the connector and turn it clockwise until it is finger-tight. You don't need any tools, and you shouldn't force it.

Attach the antenna before you power on

Without the antenna, the Gateway may not find your Wi-Fi network or your sensors. Always attach it before plugging the Gateway in.

  • Next Step: Flashing (Step 2)

docs.title: Step 2: Flashing Your Gateway
docs.text:
The Crosswalk Gateway is the "hub" for your Apex Crosswalk sensors. Before it joins your home, you'll install the latest firmware on it.

Why we Flash First

To ensure you have the absolute latest features and the most secure, privacy-focused version of our local software, we start every setup by quickly updating the device's firmware. This ensures your hardware is running the best possible version of the Crosswalk Gateway before it joins your home.

Browser Requirement

You must use Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac to flash your device. We do not support other browsers for flashing.

Reading this on your phone? Open docs.apexsensorlabs.com on your computer and go to Crosswalk Gateway → Step 2: Flashing.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Crosswalk Gateway Hub
  • USB-C Cable
  • Computer with Chrome or Edge installed.

docs.title: Finding the BOOT Button
docs.text: To flash the Gateway, you need to hold down its BOOT button while you plug it in. The button is inside the case, so take the lid off the case first. There are two small buttons on the board. The BOOT button is the one closest to the USB-C port, circled below.

docs.title: Flashing Procedure
docs.text:
1. Connect: Hold down the BOOT button, circled in red above. With the button held down, plug the Gateway into your computer's USB port. Let go of the boot button once it's plugged in.

  2. Start Flash: Click the Install button below.

    Install Crosswalk Gateway

  3. Select Device: A small window will pop up. Select the entry that says "USB Serial" or "Enhanced COM Port" and click Connect.

  4. Install Gateway Firmware: Click Install Crosswalk Gateway

  5. Click Confirm: Click Confirm to finish installation.

  6. Wait: Do not unplug the device until the screen says "Installation Complete".

  7. Finish: Unplug the Gateway and put the lid back on the case. Your Gateway is now ready to connect to your home network.

Beta firmware (for testers)

Beta firmware lets you try new features before they're released. It's still being tested, so it may have bugs. If you're setting up your Gateway for the first time, use the regular install button above.

Current beta: 1.3.0. Adds a Mounting setting for each sensor, for doorways taller than a standard door: Standard (6'8" door), 7 ft door, 8 ft door, and Custom (advanced).

Put your Gateway and all your sensors on the beta together

A beta Gateway doesn't work with sensors on the regular firmware, and a regular Gateway doesn't work with beta sensors. If you install the beta on your Gateway, install it on every sensor too. See Sensor Flashing.

To install it, follow the same steps above, but click this button in step 2 instead:

Install Crosswalk Gateway (Beta)

Once you're on the beta:

  • Turn off update checks: In the dashboard, open Settings, find the Firmware section, and untick Auto-check for updates.
  • "Update available: 1.2.13" means going back: The Gateway offers the regular release as an update, because it's a different version from the beta. Clicking Install Update takes the Gateway off the beta, and your beta sensors will stop working with it until you put them back on the regular firmware too. Only click it if you're leaving the beta.
  • New betas come by USB only: Your Gateway won't receive future betas on its own. To get one, install it again with the button above.
  • Going back to the regular firmware: Put the Gateway back by clicking Install Update when it shows "Update available: 1.2.13" (press Check for Updates first if auto-check is off), or with the regular install button above. Then reinstall the regular firmware on every sensor from the Sensor Flashing page.
  • Next Step: Connecting & Setup (Step 3)

docs.title: MQTT Reference
docs.text:
This page lists every MQTT topic the Crosswalk Gateway uses. It's for people who want to use their room counts outside Home Assistant, for example in Node-RED, openHAB, Hubitat, or their own scripts.

Using Home Assistant? You don't need this page

Home Assistant finds your Gateway, rooms, and sensors automatically. Everything on this page is already set up for you.

Requires an MQTT broker

The Gateway sends its data to an MQTT broker. It doesn't include one. You'll need a broker running on your network, such as the Mosquitto broker add-on in Home Assistant, or Mosquitto on another computer. Connect the Gateway to it in Step 3: Connecting & Setup.

If the MQTT settings are left blank, the Gateway runs on its own and nothing on this page is available. You can still use the apex.local dashboard.

Firmware version

Items marked 1.2.13+ need Gateway firmware 1.2.13 or later. Everything else works on all current firmware. See Updating Firmware to check your version.

docs.title: How Topics Are Named
docs.text:
Every topic starts with apex/. Rooms and sensors each have their own ID in the topic:

ID What it is Example <room> The room's name when you first added it, in lowercase with spaces and symbols turned into hyphens. If two rooms would get the same ID, the second gets -2 added. "Living Room" → living-room <sensor> The sensor's MAC, shown on its card in the dashboard's Sensors tab. Always 12 lowercase characters. 14c19fe1e574

Renaming a room keeps its ID

Renaming a room only changes the name you see. Its topic stays the same, so your automations keep working. Deleting a room and adding it again creates a new ID.

One Gateway per broker

Topics don't include the Gateway's name, so two Gateways connected to the same broker would overwrite each other's data.

docs.title: Gateway Status
docs.text: Topic Payload apex/status online while the Gateway is connected, offline if it drops off. The broker sends offline for the Gateway if it loses power or Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Room Topics
docs.text:
Published for every room, whenever its count changes.

Topic Payload apex/room/<room>/count Number of people in the room, e.g. 2. Never goes below 0. apex/room/<room>/occupied ON when the count is above 0, otherwise OFF. apex/room/<room>/last_changed When the count last changed. See Timestamps.

docs.title: Sensor Topics
docs.text:
Published for every paired sensor.

Topic Payload apex/sensor/<sensor>/battery Battery level in percent, e.g. 87. Battery-Powered sensors only. apex/sensor/<sensor>/voltage_mv Battery voltage in millivolts, e.g. 3912. Battery-Powered sensors only. apex/sensor/<sensor>/rssi Signal strength in dBm, e.g. -62. Closer to 0 is stronger. apex/sensor/<sensor>/last_seen When the Gateway last heard from the sensor. See Timestamps. apex/sensor/<sensor>/invert ON if the counting direction is inverted, otherwise OFF. apex/sensor/<sensor>/door_left Left door state as reported by the sensor: ON = open, OFF = closed. apex/sensor/<sensor>/door_right Right door state as reported by the sensor: ON = open, OFF = closed. apex/sensor/<sensor>/fw_version The sensor's firmware version, e.g. 0x03.

docs.title: System Topics
docs.text: Topic Payload apex/system/total_occupancy Total people across all rooms, e.g. 3. apex/system/sensor_count Number of sensors currently online. apex/system/pairing ON while the Gateway is accepting new sensors, otherwise OFF. 1.2.13+

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Publish to these topics to control the Gateway.

Topic Payload What it does apex/room/<room>/reset/cmd Anything Sets the room's count to 0. apex/room/<room>/adjust/up/cmd Anything Adds 1 to the room's count. apex/room/<room>/adjust/down/cmd Anything Subtracts 1 from the room's count (it won't go below 0). apex/sensor/<sensor>/invert/cmd ON or OFF Inverts the sensor's counting direction, or sets it back. apex/sensor/<sensor>/repair/cmd Anything Tells the sensor to pair again, the same as Force Re-pair on the dashboard. apex/system/reset_all/cmd Anything Sets every room's count to 0. apex/system/pairing/cmd ON or OFF Turns pairing on or off. Pairing turns off on its own after 30 minutes, or if the Gateway restarts. Sending ON while it's already on restarts the 30 minutes. 1.2.13+ apex/system/time/cmd Unix time in seconds, e.g. 1763200000 Sets the Gateway's clock. Optional: you don't normally need this. See Timestamps. 1.2.13+

Don't send commands with the retain flag

The Gateway's own data is retained by the broker so new apps get current values straight away. Commands must not be retained. A retained command is sent to the Gateway again every time it reconnects, so a retained reset/cmd would zero that room after every restart.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
Format changed in 1.2.13

Before 1.2.13, last_changed and last_seen were a plain number. They're now a small JSON message. If you read these topics in Node-RED or a script, update it when you upgrade. Home Assistant handles the change for you.

On 1.2.13+, last_changed and last_seen look like this:

{"t": 1763200000, "age": 42}
Field Meaning t When it happened, as Unix time in seconds. 0 if the Gateway doesn't know the time yet. age How many seconds before this message it happened. -1 if it happened before the Gateway last restarted.

To get the time: use t if it isn't 0. Otherwise, if age isn't -1, subtract age from the time the message arrived. If t is 0 and age is -1, the time is unknown.

The Gateway sets its clock on its own, from the internet or from your browser when you open the dashboard, so you don't need to set anything up. apex/system/time/cmd is there if you'd rather set the clock yourself.

Earlier firmware

Before 1.2.13, the Gateway has no real clock, so last_changed and last_seen aren't reliable. Use the time your broker receives the message instead.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These use the mosquitto_sub and mosquitto_pub command-line tools. Replace 192.168.1.10 with your broker's address, and add -u <username> -P <password> if your broker needs a login.

Watch everything the Gateway sends:

mosquitto_sub -h 192.168.1.10 -t 'apex/#' -v

Watch one room's count:

mosquitto_sub -h 192.168.1.10 -t 'apex/room/living-room/count'

Reset a room to 0:

mosquitto_pub -h 192.168.1.10 -t 'apex/room/living-room/reset/cmd' -m 'reset'

Invert a sensor's direction:

mosquitto_pub -h 192.168.1.10 -t 'apex/sensor/14c19fe1e574/invert/cmd' -m 'ON'

In Node-RED, an mqtt in node subscribed to apex/room/+/count gives you every room's count, with the room ID in msg.topic.

docs.title: Home Assistant Discovery
docs.text:
The Gateway also publishes the setup messages Home Assistant uses to find it, under the homeassistant/ prefix. If your system uses a different prefix, change Discovery prefix in the MQTT section of the dashboard's Settings tab. Other systems can ignore these messages.

On 1.2.13+, the Gateway also listens on homeassistant/status (or <your prefix>/status). Whenever Home Assistant restarts and sends online there, the Gateway sends all of its current data again.

Diagnostic topics

Each sensor also reports battery-life statistics under apex/sensor/<sensor>/: wakes, awake_ms, queue_len, cum_wakes, cum_events, cum_awake_ms, and cold_boots. They're used by Apex support to investigate battery drain, and they may change between firmware versions, so don't build automations on them.

  • Gateway Troubleshooting
  • Back to Home Page

docs.title: Step 3: Connecting and Setup
docs.text: Now you need to connect your Gateway to your home Wi-Fi and set up its connection to your smart home app.

docs.title: 1. Wi-Fi Configuration
docs.text:
1. Power On: Plug your Gateway into a USB power adapter in a wall outlet. It doesn't need to stay connected to your computer. Give it a moment to start up.

  2. Find the Hotspot: On your phone or computer, open your Wi-Fi settings. Look for a network starting with Apex-Setup — each Gateway adds its own four-character suffix, so yours will look something like Apex-Setup-ca3f.

  3. Connect: Join that network. Once connected, open a web browser on your phone and visit "http://192.168.4.1".

  4. Enter Credentials: Pick your home's 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network from the list, type your password, and click Connect.

    List says 'No networks found'?

    Give the Gateway a few seconds to finish scanning and reload the page. You can also type your network name into the top box by hand.

  5. Connected: A message appears below the Connect button saying Connected!, with two addresses for your Gateway: http://apex.local and a number address such as http://192.168.1.50. Write down the number address, since you may need it in the next section. The Gateway then restarts and joins your home network.

    The message is red, but it worked

    The Connected! message is shown in red text. As long as it says Connected!, your Gateway has joined your Wi-Fi.

    Saw a different message?

    Sometimes your phone drops off the Apex-Setup network before the Gateway can reply. The page will then say The gateway is joining your WiFi. That's normal: carry on to the next step. If the Gateway doesn't show up within a minute, see Gateway Doesn't Show Up After Wi-Fi Setup.

  6. Reconnect Your Phone: Switch your phone back to your home Wi-Fi network.

docs.title: 2. The Apex Dashboard
docs.text:
Your Gateway has its own "Control Panel" that you can access from any browser in your house.

  1. Open Browser: Type http://apex.local into your browser's address bar.

    Trouble finding the dashboard?

    Some phones (especially Android) and routers don't support apex.local. Type the number address from the Connected! message instead, e.g. http://192.168.1.50. If you didn't write it down, look for 'Crosswalk-Gateway' in your router's device list to find it.

  2. The Main Screen: You should now see the Apex Gateway dashboard, with the Rooms, Sensors, Settings, and Status tabs across the top.

docs.title: 3. Smart Home Connection (MQTT)
docs.text:
To send the person counts to Home Assistant or other apps, you need to set up "MQTT".

  1. Go to Settings: On the dashboard, click the Settings tab at the top, then scroll down to find the MQTT section.

  2. Type Broker Info: Enter your MQTT Broker's address (usually the IP of your Home Assistant server).

    Test before you save

    Click Test Connection to check your details before saving. If the test fails, double-check the address, username, and password. Fixing them now saves you a restart.

  3. Save: Click Save. The Gateway restarts to apply your settings.

    'Reconnecting' message won't go away?

    While the Gateway restarts, the dashboard may show a Reconnecting message that stays on screen even after the Gateway is back. This is normal. Wait a minute, then close the message.

  4. Check the Connection: Click the Status tab at the top of the dashboard. Next to MQTT, it should say Connected.

    If it says Disconnected, see MQTT Connection Problems.

docs.title: 4. Gateway Connected
docs.text:
Your Apex Crosswalk Gateway is now connected and set up. It uses the Home Assistant discovery message by default, so your Gateway and your Crosswalk sensors appear automatically in Home Assistant or any smart home hub of your choice. Go check it out in your smart home!

Your Apex Gateway lists information for you here to include 'Total Occupancy'. This is an aggregation of all room counts between all of your Crosswalk Sensors. If two people are in your 'Office' and one person is in the 'Living Room' this count would be 3. This also lists and links to all of your Crosswalk sensor devices. You can easily click 'Reset All Rooms' to revert the room counts to 0 across your entire setup.

Not using Home Assistant?

Systems like Node-RED, openHAB, or Hubitat can read your counts straight from MQTT. See the MQTT Reference for every topic the Gateway uses.

docs.title: 5. Add Rooms
docs.text:
Now we need to add and configure rooms before adding a sensor. Go to the Rooms tab at the top and add some rooms!

  1. Add a Room: Type in the room name and click 'Add'

  2. Configure Rooms: Now that you have rooms set up, you can reset the counts, increment, decrement the room count, rename the room, or delete the room. This all syncs over MQTT to your smart home setup.

  3. Set up Sensors: Now it's time to go set up your Crosswalk sensors. Click the link below to start setting up a sensor.

  • Next Step: Set up your Sensors
  • Keeping the Gateway Updated

docs.title: Crosswalk Gateway Troubleshooting
docs.text: If your Gateway is having trouble connecting to Wi-Fi or coordinating sensors, follow these steps.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
1. Immediately after flashing, it should host its own Wi-Fi connection. Make sure you switch to this using your phone.
  2. Once connected, visit http://192.168.4.1 in your phone's web browser. This will allow you to set up the Wi-Fi for the gateway.
  3. Once this is done, remember to re-connect to your home's Wi-Fi on your phone.

docs.title: Gateway Doesn't Show Up After Wi-Fi Setup
docs.text:
If you've reconnected your phone to your home Wi-Fi but the dashboard won't load a minute or so after setup:

  1. Try the Number Address: If the setup page showed a number address such as http://192.168.1.50, try that instead of http://apex.local. Some phones, especially Android, can't open apex.local.
  2. Check for the Setup Network: Look at your phone's Wi-Fi list. If the Apex-Setup network is back, the Gateway couldn't join your Wi-Fi, most likely because of a wrong password. Connect to it, visit http://192.168.4.1, and enter your network name and password again, making sure you pick a 2.4GHz network.
  3. Power Cycle: If neither works, unplug the Gateway, wait 10 seconds, and plug it back in. It will try your saved Wi-Fi details again.

docs.title: I Can't Open apex.local
docs.text:
1. Check Connection: Make sure your computer or phone is on the same Wi-Fi network as the Gateway.
  2. Use the IP Address: If http://apex.local fails, look at your router's device list for "Crosswalk-Gateway" and type its IP address (e.g., http://192.168.1.50) into your browser.

docs.title: MQTT Connection Problems
docs.text:
To check your MQTT connection, open the Status tab on your apex.local dashboard and look at the MQTT line.

Stuck on 'Reconnecting'?

Saving your MQTT settings restarts the Gateway. The dashboard may keep showing a Reconnecting message even after the Gateway is back. Close the message and check the Status tab instead.

If the Status tab says MQTT is Disconnected:

  1. Verify Broker IP: Ensure the IP address of your Home Assistant (or broker) hasn't changed.
  2. Check Credentials: Double-check your Username and Password in the MQTT section of the Settings tab.
  3. Port 1883: Ensure your broker is listening on the standard port (1883) and is not blocked by a firewall.
  4. Test Before Saving: In the MQTT section, enter your settings and click Test Connection before you click Save. Saving restarts the Gateway, so testing first lets you catch mistakes without waiting for a restart.

docs.title: Firmware Updates
docs.text:
The Gateway updates itself from its own dashboard — see Updating Firmware. If an update is interrupted and the Gateway no longer comes back online, you can always recover it by reflashing over USB from the Flashing page.

Restart

Most Gateway issues can be fixed by simply unplugging it for 10 seconds and plugging it back in to refresh the network connection.

docs.title: Updating Firmware
docs.text:
Your Crosswalk Gateway updates itself over your home network. You do not need to plug it back into a computer or use the install button again.

Current Version

The latest Gateway firmware is 1.2.13. Your Gateway shows the version it is currently running on the dashboard.

What's new in 1.2.13
  • Easier pairing: Enable Pairing replaces the 60-second pairing window. Pairing stays on while you add as many sensors as you like, until you turn it off (or 30 minutes pass).
  • Real times: "Last Seen" and "Last Changed" now show the correct date and time in Home Assistant, instead of January 1970. There's nothing to set up.
  • Smoother Wi-Fi setup: the setup page no longer shows "Load failed" after you connect, and it shows the Gateway's number address as well as apex.local.
  • Home Assistant restarts: the Gateway sends all its data again whenever Home Assistant restarts.
  • For MQTT users: timestamp topics have a new format, and pairing can be turned on or off over MQTT. See the MQTT Reference.

docs.title: 1. Open the Dashboard
docs.text:
Type http://apex.local into any browser on your home network.

Trouble finding the dashboard?

If http://apex.local doesn't load, look for Crosswalk-Gateway in your router's device list and type its IP address into your browser instead.

docs.title: 2. Check for an Update
docs.text: Go to Settings and open the firmware update section. The Gateway checks with Apex Sensor Labs and tells you whether a newer version is available.

docs.title: 3. Install
docs.text:
Start the update and leave the Gateway alone. It downloads the new firmware, installs it, and restarts on its own.

Keep it powered

Do not unplug the Gateway while it is updating. Interrupting an update partway through can leave the device needing a USB reflash to recover.

docs.title: 4. Confirm
docs.text:
Once the Gateway restarts, reload http://apex.local and check that the version number on the dashboard has changed.

If the dashboard doesn't come back after a couple of minutes, unplug the Gateway for 10 seconds and plug it back in.

docs.title: What About the Sensors?
docs.text: Crosswalk sensors do not update over the air. To update a sensor, connect it to your computer over USB and use the install button on the Sensor Flashing page, exactly as you did during first-time setup.

docs.title: Beta Firmware
docs.text:
Want to try new features early? Beta firmware is available for the Gateway and both sensor versions. It's installed over USB from the Beta firmware section at the bottom of the Gateway Flashing and Sensor Flashing pages. It's never sent to your Gateway automatically.

The Gateway and sensors must all be on the beta, or all on the regular firmware. They don't work together when mixed.

On the beta? Read this before clicking Install Update

A Gateway running beta firmware will show "Update available: 1.2.13". That's the regular release, not a newer version. Clicking Install Update takes your Gateway off the beta, and your beta sensors will stop working with it until you reinstall the regular firmware on them too. To stop the message appearing, untick Auto-check for updates in the Firmware section of Settings.

  • Gateway Troubleshooting
  • Back to Home Page

docs.title: Getting Started with Crosswalk Gateway
docs.text: The Crosswalk Gateway is the heart of your person-counting ecosystem. It acts as the bridge between your battery-powered Crosswalk sensors (using ESP-NOW) and your smart home controller (over MQTT).

docs.title: Unboxing
docs.text:
The Crosswalk Gateway is the central coordinator for your person-counting sensors.

  • 1x Crosswalk Gateway: Powered by an ESP32-S3.
  • 1x Crosswalk Gateway Case: Fits the Crosswalk Gateway board
  • 1x u.FL/IPEX to SMA adapter: Already installed inside the case. Connects the Gateway board to the antenna.
  • 1x 2.4GHz Antenna: For Wi-Fi and ESP-NOW. You'll screw this on in Step 1.
  • USB-C Cable NOT included: You'll need one to flash the Gateway and to power it afterwards.

docs.title: Setup Process
docs.text:
To get started, follow our linear walkthrough to set up your Gateway.

  1. Attach the Antenna: Screw the antenna onto the Gateway.
  2. Flashing: Install the latest firmware.
  3. Connecting & Setup: Connect to Wi-Fi and MQTT.

You'll need a computer for Step 2

To flash the Gateway, you'll need Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac. You'll use your phone in Step 3 to connect the Gateway to your Wi-Fi.

Dependency

You must complete this Gateway setup before attempting to install your Crosswalk Sensors. Sensors will not be able to transmit data until a Gateway is online and within range.

  • Start Step 1: Attach the Antenna

docs.title: Step 2: Pairing & Configuration
docs.text: Before you mount the sensor, you need to link it to your Gateway. Keep the sensor near you for this step, since you'll power it on while the Gateway is waiting for it.

docs.title: 1. Linking to the Gateway
docs.text:
To add a new sensor, you first turn on pairing on the Gateway. While pairing is on, the Gateway accepts new sensors, so you can add one sensor or several in one go.

  1. Open Dashboard: Navigate to http://apex.local on your browser. Go to the Sensors tab.

  2. Enable Pairing: In the Add Sensor card, click Enable Pairing. A banner appears saying Pairing enabled. Power on your new sensors.

    No need to rush

    Pairing stays on until you turn it off. As a safety measure it also switches off by itself after 30 minutes, shown as auto-off on the banner. Click Keep open 30 min if you need more time.

  3. Activate the Sensor: While pairing is on, power on your Crosswalk sensor. It will automatically start up and pair with the Gateway.

    Battery-PoweredHardwired

    The battery is already inside the case, but it isn't plugged in. To connect it:

    1. Slide the back cover of the case partway open. You only need enough room to reach the battery plug, so don't take it all the way off.
    2. Plug the battery's small white connector into the matching socket on the board.
    3. Slide the back cover closed again.

    Watch the dashboard, not the sensor

    Once it's running on battery, the sensor keeps all of its lights off to save power — so there is no light to tell you it is awake and working. The Gateway dashboard is where you confirm pairing.

    Plug a USB-C cable into the sensor and into a USB power adapter.

    Watch the dashboard, not the sensor

    The red power light and the green light come on as soon as the sensor has power. They only mean the board is powered, not that it has paired. The Gateway dashboard is where you confirm pairing.

    • Note: The sensor will scan for the Gateway automatically.

  4. Success: When the sensor pairs, its code appears on the banner under Paired so far, and a new card for it appears in the sensor list.

  5. Disable Pairing: If you have more sensors to add, power them on now. They'll pair the same way. When you're done, click Disable Pairing.

    Why turn pairing off?

    While pairing is on, any Crosswalk sensor in range can join your Gateway. Turning it off when you're finished keeps your setup to just your own sensors. Pairing also turns off whenever the Gateway restarts.

  6. Home Assistant: Check out your new sensor in Home Assistant!

    The Apex Crosswalk Gateway should now show a connected sensor as well.

    Check out a Room.

    Now go look at the sensor.

docs.title: 2. Device Settings
docs.text:
Now you can customize how this sensor behaves in your home. Go back to the Apex Gateway web page.

  1. Find Your Sensor: On the Sensors tab, find your new sensor in the list. A new sensor is named Sensor followed by a four-character code, such as Sensor e574, and shows an online badge.

  2. Rename It: On that sensor's card, click the Rename button below the Mode menu. Give it a clear name like "Office Door" or "Office - Bathroom Door", then confirm.

Leave the Mode as 'Not configured' for now

You'll choose the counting mode in the next step, once the sensor is mounted on the doorway. Until then it won't count anyone.

  • Next Step: Mounting (Step 3)

docs.title: Step 1: Flashing Your Sensor
docs.text:
The Crosswalk Sensor is the part that goes on your door. You need to flash it before you mount it.

Why we Flash First

To ensure you have the absolute latest features and the most secure, privacy-focused version of our local software, we start every setup by quickly updating the device's firmware. This ensures your sensor is running the most battery-efficient version of our code.

Browser Requirement

You must use Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac to flash your device. We do not support other browsers for flashing.

Reading this on your phone? Open docs.apexsensorlabs.com on your computer and go to Crosswalk Sensor → Step 1: Flashing.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Crosswalk Sensor
  • USB-C Cable
  • Computer with Chrome or Edge installed.
  • Paperclip (a standard one works)

docs.title: Finding the BOOT Button
docs.text: You don't need to open the case to flash the sensor. The BOOT button sits under a small slot on the top of the case, circled below. You'll press it with the end of a paperclip. This is the same on both the Battery-Powered and Hardwired versions.

docs.title: Flashing Procedure
docs.text:
1. Connect: Push a paperclip into the BOOT slot and hold the button down. With the button held down, plug the USB-C cable into the sensor and your computer. Let go of the button once it's plugged in.

  2. Flash: Choose the tab that matches your sensor, then click its Install button.

    Battery-PoweredHardwired

    Install Crosswalk Sensor

    Install Crosswalk Sensor (Hardwired)

    Pick the Right Version

    Both versions use the same chip, so the installer can't tell them apart. Installing the wrong one won't damage anything, but your sensor won't work correctly until you install the version that matches your hardware.

  3. Wait: Do not unplug the sensor until the screen says "Installation Complete".

  4. Ready: Your sensor is now ready to be paired with your Gateway.

Beta firmware (for testers)

Beta firmware lets you try new features before they're released. It's still being tested, so it may have bugs. If you're setting up your sensor for the first time, use the regular install button above.

Current beta: lets you set the sensor's detection distance from the Gateway, for doorways taller than a standard door.

Put your Gateway and all your sensors on the beta together

A beta sensor doesn't work with a Gateway on the regular firmware, and a regular sensor doesn't work with a beta Gateway. Install the beta on your Gateway from the Gateway Flashing page, and on every sensor.

To install it, follow the same steps above, but choose the tab that matches your sensor and click its beta button in step 2 instead:

Battery-PoweredHardwired

Install Crosswalk Sensor (Beta)

Install Crosswalk Sensor (Hardwired, Beta)

Just like the regular firmware, make sure you pick the version that matches your sensor.

Going back to the regular firmware: Connect each sensor to your computer again and use the regular install button above. Sensors don't update on their own, so they stay on the beta until you do. Put your Gateway back on the regular firmware too (see Gateway Flashing).

  • Next Step: Pairing & Configuration (Step 2)

docs.title: Hardware & Pinout
docs.text:
Built something with your Crosswalk? Tell us!

We'd love to hear how you've written your own code or used your Crosswalk Sensor in a new way. Email us at contact@apexsensorlabs.com and share your project.

This page is for people who want to write their own firmware for the Crosswalk Sensor, for example with ESPHome or the Arduino IDE. It lists what's connected to each pin and how to power the distance sensors.

Advanced, and not supported

Custom firmware isn't supported by Apex Sensor Labs.

  • It won't work with the Crosswalk Gateway. The Gateway only talks to the official sensor firmware.
  • Battery life depends on your code. The official firmware sleeps between people walking past to last months on a charge. Firmware that keeps Wi-Fi on will drain the battery much faster.

You can always go back. Reinstall the official firmware from the Sensor Flashing page. Please do that before contacting support.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text:
Module ESP32-C6-MINI-1-N4 (ESP32-C6, 4 MB flash) Distance sensors 2× VL53L1X time-of-flight sensors, looking down through the doorway Motion sensor AS312 PIR Door sensors 2× AH1912 hall-effect sensors (left and right) Battery gauge MAX17048 (Battery-Powered version only) USB-C Connected to the ESP32-C6's built-in USB, for flashing and serial output. No extra driver needed. Buttons BOOT (GPIO9) and RESET

The Battery-Powered and Hardwired versions use the same board. The Hardwired version has no battery, so the battery gauge isn't powered.

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text:
GPIO Connected to Direction Notes 2 Distance sensor power switch Output LOW = on, HIGH = off. See Distance Sensor Power. 3 Motion sensor (PIR) output Input HIGH for about 2.3 seconds after motion. Can wake the ESP32-C6 from deep sleep. 4 Distance sensors I²C SDA I²C Shared by both distance sensors. Boot-mode (strapping) pin. 5 Distance sensors I²C SCL I²C Shared by both distance sensors. Boot-mode (strapping) pin. 6 Battery gauge I²C SDA I²C A separate bus from the distance sensors. 7 Battery gauge I²C SCL I²C A separate bus from the distance sensors. 18 Distance sensor 1 XSHUT Output LOW holds the sensor off. Used to give the two sensors different addresses. 19 Distance sensor 2 XSHUT Output LOW holds the sensor off. Used to give the two sensors different addresses. 21 Power LED Output HIGH = on. 22 Left door hall sensor Input LOW when a magnet is near. Enable the internal pull-up: there's no pull-up on the board. 23 Right door hall sensor Input LOW when a magnet is near. Enable the internal pull-up: there's no pull-up on the board. 9 BOOT button Input LOW when pressed. Hold it while plugging in USB to enter download mode. 12 / 13 USB D− / D+ USB Built-in USB. Don't use these as GPIO.

All other GPIOs are unused, and none are brought out to a connector.

docs.title: I²C Addresses
docs.text:
Device Bus Address VL53L1X (each) GPIO4 / GPIO5 0x29 at power-up. Both start at the same address. See below. MAX17048 GPIO6 / GPIO7 0x36

The official firmware moves the distance sensors to 0x30 and 0x32. You can use any free addresses.

docs.title: Distance Sensor Power
docs.text:
The two distance sensors run on their own switched 3.3 V supply, so they can be turned off completely while the ESP32-C6 is in deep sleep. GPIO2 controls a switch on that supply:

GPIO2 Distance sensors LOW Powered HIGH Off

LOW turns it on

It's the opposite of what most people expect. If your distance sensors don't respond at all, check that you're driving GPIO2 LOW.

What's on the switched supply: both VL53L1X sensors, plus the pull-up resistors on their I²C lines (GPIO4/5) and their XSHUT lines (GPIO18/19). Nothing else.

What's not on the switched supply: the ESP32-C6, the motion sensor, both door sensors, and the battery gauge (powered by the battery) stay powered when GPIO2 is HIGH. The power LED isn't on the switched supply either. Your code turns it on and off with GPIO21.

docs.title: Rules for Your Code
docs.text:
1. It starts off. The switch is held off until your code drives GPIO2 LOW, so the distance sensors are unpowered at boot.
  2. Wait before talking to the sensors. After driving GPIO2 LOW, wait at least 70 ms before any I²C traffic. The official firmware waits 100 ms after switching it back on.

  3. Give the sensors different addresses every time you power them up. Both start at 0x29. Hold both XSHUT pins LOW, then:

    1. Set GPIO18 HIGH, wait 5 ms, and move that sensor to a new address.
    2. Set GPIO19 HIGH, wait 5 ms, and move that sensor to a different address.

    Switching the supply off and on resets both sensors to 0x29, so repeat this after every power cycle. 4. Turning the supply off: stop ranging first, then drive both XSHUT pins LOW, then set GPIO2 HIGH. Talking to unpowered sensors just times out, and leaving XSHUT HIGH can feed power into the sensors through the pin. 5. Keep it off through deep sleep. If your code uses deep sleep, hold GPIO2 HIGH while asleep (in Arduino: rtc_gpio_hold_en(GPIO_NUM_2), and rtc_gpio_hold_dis when you wake). Otherwise the pin floats, the switch can partly turn on, and the distance sensors drain the battery while the board is asleep. 6. Don't drive GPIO4/5 LOW at boot. They're boot-mode (strapping) pins.

The distance sensors' interrupt pins aren't connected, so read them by polling.

docs.title: Example Code
docs.text:
These examples show the basics: powering the distance sensors, reading them, and reading the motion and door sensors.

ArduinoESPHome

Uses the VL53L1X library by Pololu and the SparkFun MAX1704x Fuel Gauge library, both available in the Arduino Library Manager. Select the ESP32C6 Dev Module board and turn on USB CDC On Boot to see the output over USB.

#include <Wire.h>
#include <VL53L1X.h>
#include <SparkFun_MAX1704x_Fuel_Gauge_Arduino_Library.h>

#define PIN_SENSOR_POWER 2    // LOW = distance sensors on
#define PIN_PIR          3
#define PIN_SDA          4    // distance sensors
#define PIN_SCL          5
#define PIN_GAUGE_SDA    6    // battery gauge
#define PIN_GAUGE_SCL    7
#define PIN_XSHUT_1      18
#define PIN_XSHUT_2      19
#define PIN_LED          21
#define PIN_DOOR_LEFT    22
#define PIN_DOOR_RIGHT   23

TwoWire sensorBus = TwoWire(0);
TwoWire gaugeBus  = TwoWire(1);
VL53L1X sensor1, sensor2;
SFE_MAX1704X gauge;

bool startSensor(VL53L1X& s, int xshutPin, uint8_t address) {
  digitalWrite(xshutPin, HIGH);   // release this sensor only
  delay(5);
  s.setBus(&sensorBus);
  s.setTimeout(500);
  if (!s.init()) return false;
  s.setAddress(address);          // move it off the shared 0x29
  s.startContinuous(50);
  return true;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);

  pinMode(PIN_PIR, INPUT);
  pinMode(PIN_DOOR_LEFT, INPUT_PULLUP);    // no pull-up on the board
  pinMode(PIN_DOOR_RIGHT, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(PIN_LED, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);             // on while testing; set LOW to save battery

  // Hold both distance sensors off, then power the switched supply.
  pinMode(PIN_XSHUT_1, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(PIN_XSHUT_2, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_XSHUT_1, LOW);
  digitalWrite(PIN_XSHUT_2, LOW);
  pinMode(PIN_SENSOR_POWER, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_SENSOR_POWER, LOW);     // LOW = on
  delay(100);                              // let the supply settle

  sensorBus.begin(PIN_SDA, PIN_SCL);
  sensorBus.setClock(400000);
  Serial.printf("Sensor 1: %s\n", startSensor(sensor1, PIN_XSHUT_1, 0x30) ? "ok" : "FAILED");
  Serial.printf("Sensor 2: %s\n", startSensor(sensor2, PIN_XSHUT_2, 0x32) ? "ok" : "FAILED");

  gaugeBus.begin(PIN_GAUGE_SDA, PIN_GAUGE_SCL);
  if (!gauge.begin(gaugeBus)) Serial.println("No battery gauge (normal on Hardwired)");
}

void loop() {
  Serial.printf("dist1=%u mm  dist2=%u mm  motion=%d  leftMagnet=%d  rightMagnet=%d  battery=%.0f%%\n",
                sensor1.read(), sensor2.read(),
                digitalRead(PIN_PIR),
                digitalRead(PIN_DOOR_LEFT) == LOW,
                digitalRead(PIN_DOOR_RIGHT) == LOW,
                gauge.getSOC());
  delay(200);
}

Turn the LED off on battery

This example leaves the power LED on so you can see the board is running. On the Battery-Powered version, turn it off (digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW)) once you're done testing, and before deep sleep.

This sets up the motion sensor, both door sensors, the LED, and the distance sensors' power. ESPHome doesn't have a built-in VL53L1X component, so you'll need to add one yourself as an external component. Power the sensors and set their addresses as described in Rules for Your Code.

esphome:
  name: crosswalk-custom
  on_boot:
    priority: 800
    then:
      - output.turn_on: distance_sensor_power

esp32:
  variant: esp32c6
  board: esp32-c6-devkitc-1
  framework:
    type: esp-idf

logger:
api:
ota:
  - platform: esphome
wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password

output:
  # GPIO2 is LOW = on, so invert it: "on" in ESPHome powers the sensors.
  - platform: gpio
    id: distance_sensor_power
    pin:
      number: GPIO2
      inverted: true
  - platform: gpio
    id: power_led
    pin: GPIO21

binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    name: "Motion"
    device_class: motion
    pin: GPIO3

  # The hall sensors pull LOW when a magnet is near, and need the
  # internal pull-up. Inverted so ON = magnet detected.
  - platform: gpio
    name: "Left Door Magnet"
    pin:
      number: GPIO22
      inverted: true
      mode:
        input: true
        pullup: true
  - platform: gpio
    name: "Right Door Magnet"
    pin:
      number: GPIO23
      inverted: true
      mode:
        input: true
        pullup: true

light:
  - platform: binary
    name: "Power LED"
    output: power_led

Battery-Powered sensors and ESPHome

ESPHome keeps Wi-Fi on all the time, which drains the battery quickly. ESPHome works best on the Hardwired version. On the Battery-Powered version, look at ESPHome's deep_sleep component, with the motion sensor (GPIO3) as the wake-up pin.

  • Reinstall the Official Firmware
  • Sensor Troubleshooting

docs.title: Step 3: Mounting
docs.text: Now that your sensor is paired with your Gateway, it's time to put it on your door, tell it which room or rooms to count, and test it.

docs.title: 1. Placement
docs.text:
The Crosswalk sensor uses dual sensing zones to tell which way someone is walking, so the direction you mount it matters.

  1. Mounting Height: The Crosswalk should be placed at the top of the doorframe, inside the frame, pointing down toward the floor. Place it in the middle of the doorframe, on the inside of the door, so when the door closes it should almost rest up against the sensor.

    Why the top of the frame

    The sensor looks straight down through the doorway, so it sees the top of your head and shoulders as you pass underneath. Mounting it lower, or aiming it across the doorway at body height, will cause missed and miscounted passes.

    Far away:

  2. Direction: Stand in the doorway, facing into the room you want to count people entering. Look up at where the sensor will go. The sensor's USB-C port should be on your left.

    Which room do I face?

    • Single Room: Face the room the sensor is counting.
    • Dual Room: Face the room you'll set as the Side A room on the dashboard.

docs.title: 2. Physical Installation
docs.text:
1. Attach the Mounting Strip: Take one of the adhesive mounting strips out of the sensor bag and stick it to the back of the case. Keep the second strip as a spare. The strip makes it easy to take the sensor down later for charging or servicing.

  2. Clean the Surface: Wipe the door frame with a dry cloth to ensure a good bond.

  3. Placement: Remove the backing from the mounting strip and press the sensor firmly against the frame.

  4. Power (Hardwired only): Run a USB-C cable from the sensor to a USB power adapter in a nearby outlet. The sensor needs power at all times, so choose an outlet that isn't switched off with the lights.

    Plan your cable route

    Before you stick the sensor down, make sure your USB-C cable is long enough to reach the outlet. Route it so it stays clear of the door when it opens and closes.

docs.title: 3. Set the Counting Mode
docs.text:
A newly paired sensor is set to Not configured and won't count anyone until you tell it which room or rooms it covers.

  1. Open the Sensor: On your apex.local dashboard, open the Sensors tab and find your sensor in the list.

  2. Choose a Mode: Open the Mode menu on the sensor's card and change it from Not configured to the option that fits your doorway.

    Single RoomDual Room

    Choose Single room (one tracked) when the sensor only needs to count people entering and leaving one room.

    Then pick that room from the Tracked room menu.

    Choose Dual room (between two) when the doorway sits between two rooms you're tracking, such as a hallway and a kitchen. Each pass updates both rooms at once: walk from the Hallway into the Kitchen and the Kitchen goes up by 1 while the Hallway goes down by 1.

    Then pick the room you faced when mounting the sensor as the Side A room, and the room behind you as the Side B room.

    Room menu not showing?

    If the Tracked room menu (or the Side A room and Side B room menus) doesn't appear after you change the Mode, refresh the page in your browser. The menus will appear and your Mode choice will be kept.

Why the Gateway keeps the count

The sensor itself only knows that someone walked underneath it and which way they were going. The Gateway turns that into room counts. That's why a room with several doorways can have a sensor on each one and still show one accurate total.

docs.title: 4. Verification
docs.text:
1. Walk Through: Walk through the doorway into the room being counted.

  2. Verify: Check your apex.local dashboard or your smart home app. The room's count should go up by 1.

    Here's the detection in Home Assistant:

  3. Walk Back Out: Walk back through in the opposite direction and check the count goes back down.

  4. Correct Direction: If the count goes the wrong way (e.g., counts -1 when you enter), first check that the USB-C port is on your left when you face the room being entered. If you'd rather not remount it, open the Sensors tab on the dashboard, find the sensor in the list, and click its Enable invert button. This flips the direction instantly.

docs.title: Setup Complete!
docs.text:
Your person-counting system is now live.

  • View Support & Help
  • Back to Home Page

docs.title: Crosswalk Sensor Troubleshooting
docs.text: Ensure your occupancy counts are accurate and your sensors are communicating reliably.

docs.title: Understanding the Sensor Lights
docs.text:
The Crosswalk sensor's lights are about power, not status. They never tell you whether the sensor is paired or counting — use your apex.local dashboard or your smart home app for that.

Battery-PoweredHardwired

Once it is running on battery, the sensor keeps every light off so that nothing drains the battery.

LED Color When What it Means 🟡 Yellow Plugged into USB Battery is charging. 🟢 Green Plugged into USB Battery is fully charged. 🔴 Red When you first plug in USB Separate power light — the board has power. It switches off once the sensor enters deep sleep. ⚫ No Lights Running on battery Normal. All lights stay off to save battery.

No lights is normal

On battery power there is no light to tell you the sensor is on or working — this is intentional, and it is how the sensor lasts months on a charge. The only place to check whether a sensor is awake, paired, and counting is your apex.local dashboard or your smart home app.

The Hardwired sensor never sleeps, so its lights stay on whenever it has power.

LED Color When What it Means 🔴 Red Always, while powered The board has power. 🟢 Green Always, while powered Normal. This is the charging light, and it shows green even though there is no battery. ⚫ No Lights Any time The sensor has no power. Check the USB-C cable and power adapter.

docs.title: Installer Can't Find the Sensor
docs.text:
If you click Install and your sensor doesn't appear in the list, or the install fails right away:

  1. Use the BOOT Button: Unplug the sensor. Push a paperclip into the BOOT slot on top of the case and hold it down, then plug the USB-C cable back in. Let go once it's plugged in, then click Install again. See Flashing for a photo of the slot.
  2. Check the Browser: Flashing only works in Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge on a Windows PC or Mac. If the install button is missing, or shows a message about your browser, open this page in Chrome or Edge on your computer.
  3. Check the Cable: Some USB-C cables only carry power, not data. If the sensor still doesn't appear, try a different cable.

docs.title: Count is Backwards or Wrong
docs.text:
If the room count increases when you leave and decreases when you enter:

  1. Check the Direction: Stand in the doorway facing the room being entered (the Side A room for Dual Room sensors). The sensor's USB-C port should be on your left. If it's on your right, either remount the sensor the other way around or use Digital Invert below.

  2. Digital Invert: Go to your apex.local dashboard, open the Sensors tab, find the sensor in the list, and click its Enable invert button. This will instantly fix the direction without you needing to move the hardware. You can also do this in Home Assistant, from the sensor's device page.

  3. Clear Path: Make sure the door doesn't block the sensor when it's open. The sensor needs a clear "line of sight" straight down through the doorway.

  4. Mounting Position: The sensor must sit at the top of the doorframe pointing down at the floor, in the middle of the opening. If it has been mounted lower down or angled across the doorway, it will miss passes. See Mounting for placement.

docs.title: Sensor Won't Pair
docs.text:
1. Pairing On: Make sure pairing is turned on before you power the sensor on. On the dashboard's Sensors tab, the banner should say Pairing enabled. If it doesn't, click Enable Pairing. Pairing switches off after 30 minutes and whenever the Gateway restarts, so check it's still on.
  2. Power Cycle: While pairing is on, unplug the sensor's power and plug it back in. On the Battery-Powered version, slide the back cover partway open and unplug and replug the battery connector. On the Hardwired version, unplug and replug the USB-C cable. The sensor's lights don't show pairing, so watch the dashboard for confirmation instead.
  3. Proximity: Bring the sensor into the same room as the Gateway just for the initial pairing.

docs.title: Power Loss & Battery Changes
docs.text:
If your sensor's battery dies or you lose power to your house, don't worry!

  • No Re-Pairing Needed: The Gateway remembers your sensors. Once you charge the sensor or the power comes back on, the sensor will automatically find the Gateway again.
  • Auto-Sync: You do not need to turn on pairing again for sensors you have already set up.

docs.title: Battery Draining Quickly
docs.text:
This section applies to the Battery-Powered version only.

Charge the sensor by plugging it into USB and waiting for the light to turn from 🟡 Yellow to 🟢 Green.

If a charge isn't lasting as long as you expect:

  1. Check the Link: A sensor that struggles to reach the Gateway has to retry, and retries cost power. Confirm the sensor is reporting reliably on the dashboard.
  2. Move the Gateway Closer: If the doorway is far from the Gateway, or there are several walls between them, relocating the Gateway can make a noticeable difference.
  3. Busy Doorways: A very high-traffic doorway wakes the sensor more often and will shorten the interval between charges.
  • Gateway Troubleshooting
  • View Support & Help
